traveler: Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer-Lytton, 1st Baron Lytton
title: The Dark and Stormy Night: Knebworth, the City of the Dead, and the Word Vril
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Norfolk Name and the Lytton Name

stops.name: 31 Baker Street, the third son
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Victorian Web chronology supplies the street number, the Dictionary of National Biography only London
stops.campa: In a house in Baker Street a third son is born to General William Earle Bulwer and Elizabeth Barbara Lytton, and the two names in that pairing pull at him for seventy years. They christen him Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer, which is not yet the name he will die under. The Bulwers are Norfolk soldiers with land at Heydon and Wood Dalling, and that land goes to eldest sons. The Lyttons are Hertfordshire gentry with a house called Knebworth and, in this generation, a single heiress who holds both the purse and the affection in one fist. The heiress is his mother.
suggested_refs: The Marylebone terraces of Baker Street as they stood in 1803
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'

stops.name: Heydon Hall, Norfolk, the general dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the Victorian Web chronology; Britannica gives only 'when the boy was four'
stops.campa: He is four years old when General Bulwer dies and the Norfolk estates pass entire to the eldest son, as law and custom require. Heydon Hall and Wood Dalling stay in the family and stay his brother's. The younger boys keep the name and nothing under it. Elizabeth Barbara takes her children to London and becomes from this July the one fixed authority of his childhood: she picks his schools, reads his verses, withholds her money and restores it. She will outlive her husband by thirty-six years.
suggested_refs: Heydon Hall and the Bulwer property at Wood Dalling, the inheritance that went to the elder brother
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: Fulham, the school of Dr Ruddock
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; month and day not recorded
stops.campa: His mother begins the restless sequence of schools that runs through his boyhood, and the first of them is Dr Ruddock's establishment at Fulham. He is small, clever, often ill, and unhappy in company, a boy who reads faster than he is taught and says so. No school holds him long, because his mother removes him from any arrangement that chafes. What he gets instead of an education is his own reading and a succession of tutors chosen to suit him. Which of the two she was protecting, a delicate child or an exceptional one, the record of these years does not settle.
suggested_refs: The private academies of Fulham in the 1810s
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology', citing the Dictionary of National Biography

stops.name: Rottingdean, the vicarage school above the chalk
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the Oxford DNB, which has him arriving 'at eleven' and leaving September 1818; the Victorian Web dates the stay from 1812
stops.campa: At eleven he is sent down to the Sussex coast, where Dr Thomas Hooker, vicar of Rottingdean since 1792, keeps a school in his own vicarage house above the chalk. Henry Manning, the future cardinal, is among the boys. Four years pass in the schoolroom under the vicarage roof. In September 1818 Hooker writes to Mrs Bulwer Lytton to say plainly that he has nothing further to teach her son, which is neither expulsion nor failure, and the boy is taken home. He is fifteen.
suggested_refs: The vicarage at Rottingdean, Dr Hooker's schoolroom, and its most famous pair of pupils
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'

stops.name: Ealing, reading with the Reverend Charles Wallington
stops.date_confidence: the Oxford DNB gives 1819 to 1821 for the tutelage; the Victorian Web fixes on the summer of 1820, a point inside that span
stops.campa: For two years he reads with the Reverend Charles Wallington at Ealing, and this is the education that takes. Wallington hands him the classics and lets him love them, and does what no schoolmaster before him had done by telling the boy to publish what he writes. There is a girl at Ealing in these years too, loved and lost, who writes to him from her deathbed; he is seventeen when the letter comes. In the same parish and the same years, Henry Angelo, who had taught Byron to fence, puts a foil in his hand.
suggested_refs: Henry Angelo's fencing academy, which trained Byron and then Byron's imitator
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'
The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: London, Ismael in print
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; April given by the Victorian Web chronology
stops.campa: The volume appears: Ismael, an Oriental Tale, with Other Poems, by a boy of sixteen, printed at his mother's expense and on his tutor's urging. Some catalogues render the title Ishmael. It is Byron thinned and reheated, and he knows it well before anyone tells him so. What is fixed here, before he is out of the schoolroom, is not the verse but the habit of converting whatever he feels into pages that can be sold. He is sixteen years old and has a book with his name on it, paid for by his mother.
suggested_refs: Ismael: An Oriental Tale, with Other Poems (1820), the sixteen-year-old's first book
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

segments.name: Cambridge, Ullswater, and the Grave of a Dream

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge, going up
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Oxford DNB has him going up in January, which is Lent term; the Victorian Web chronology says Easter term 1822. Year not in dispute
stops.campa: He goes up at eighteen and a half, finds Trinity stiffly academic and himself unfitted to it, and stays one term. He moves across to Trinity Hall as a fellow-commoner, a rank that buys a better table and imposes no obligation to work. What he does with the years instead is talk: secretary of the Cambridge Union, then treasurer, then president, in rooms where the arguing is the whole of the curriculum. In 1823 a Cambridge firm prints his second volume of imitative verse, Delmour, or the Tale of a Sylphid.
suggested_refs: The fellow-commoners' table at Trinity Hall; the minute books of the Cambridge Union
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'
The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'
Dictionary of National Biography 1885-1900, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'

stops.name: Ullswater, the night on the tomb
stops.date_confidence: the Oxford DNB places it in the long vacation of 1824; month within that vacation not specified
stops.campa: In the long vacation he rides north to Ullswater, to the grave of the girl he had loved at Ealing, the one who wrote to him as she was dying. He passes the night on her tomb. Then he stays on in the Lake District for weeks alone, in a self-conscious philosophical solitude he is at that same moment writing into Erasmus Falkland, hero of a first novel then in draft on his table. His grandson's Life of him gives the chapter its title: The Grave of a Dream, 1824. Half a century later, in Kenelm Chillingly, he sends another young man to another such grave.
suggested_refs: V. A. Lytton's Life of his grandfather, chapter titled 'The Grave of a Dream. 1824.'
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'
Victor Alexander Lytton, The Life of Edward Bulwer, First Lord Lytton

stops.name: Cambridge, the Chancellor's Gold Medal
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: The Chancellor's Gold Medal for English verse goes to his poem Sculpture. It is the only academic honour he ever wins, and he mentions it for the rest of his life. The degree follows the next year, taken from Trinity Hall, where the fellow-commoners dine at the high table and are examined by nobody. He comes away from Cambridge with the medal, an appetite for debt, an army commission bought and never used, and no profession. His whole income is his mother's allowance.
suggested_refs: Sculpture, the prize poem of 1825, and the Chancellor's Gold Medal
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: Faubourg Saint-Germain, Paris, the salons
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Victorian Web places the Paris months across 1825 and the spring of 1826
stops.campa: He crosses to Paris and is taken up by the Restoration salons of the Faubourg Saint-Germain, where the Marquise de la Rochejaquelein receives him and he falls in love with one of her daughters. He is twenty-two, in a foreign drawing room, spending money that is not his and learning from the inside what a great salon looks like. His mother, an implacable anti-Catholic, ends the attachment by letter from England. Whether the daughter was told the reason, or only told no, nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The hotels of the Faubourg Saint-Germain under the Restoration
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'

stops.name: Versailles, riding in the woods
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Oxford DNB has Weeds and Wild Flowers privately printed later in 1825, the Victorian Web dates it 1826
stops.campa: Cut off from the Rochejaquelein house, he moves out to Versailles and takes the solitude he prefers to company, riding alone in the park and the woods, reading Rousseau and Mill, and finishing a volume of Byronic and satirical verse that he prints privately as Weeds and Wild Flowers. He is rehearsing the pose he will sell by the thousand within three years: the fashionable young man withdrawn from a world he understands better than it understands him. On the twenty-fifth of April 1826 he goes back to London.
suggested_refs: Weeds and Wild Flowers, privately printed, written in the woods at Versailles
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'
The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

segments.name: Woodcot, Rosina, and the Silver Fork

stops.name: Woodcot House, Oxfordshire, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: the Oxford DNB, the Wikipedia article on Rosina, and the Dictionary of Irish Biography all give 29 August; the Victorian Web chronology gives 30 August. No venue corroborated
stops.campa: He marries Rosina Doyle Wheeler, an Irish beauty with no fortune, against his mother's declared will. Mrs Bulwer Lytton refuses to attend the ceremony and stops his allowance in the same stroke. The couple set up house at Woodcot, in Oxfordshire six miles from Reading, an imposing residence whose rent and upkeep account for very nearly their whole combined income. From this year he writes for money, because there is no other money. He is twenty-four, married, and disinherited in practice if not in law.
suggested_refs: Woodcot House near Woodcote, Oxfordshire, the first married household
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'
The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'
Dictionary of Irish Biography, 'Rosina Bulwer Lytton'

stops.name: Woodcot House, the year of Pelham
stops.date_confidence: Emily's birth attested to June 1828 in the Oxford DNB; the publication month of Pelham not recorded in reachable sources
stops.campa: Their daughter Emily is born in June, and in the same year Pelham, or the Adventures of a Gentleman goes out and makes him famous. It is a dandy's memoir with a murder inside it, and fashionable London reads it as an instruction manual and dresses itself in black. The Disowned follows within months and Devereux the year after. He is paid nine hundred pounds for the one and fifteen hundred for the other, sums that make a working novelist out of a man who had expected to live on an allowance.
suggested_refs: Pelham (1828), the silver-fork novel that dressed a generation in black
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'
The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: 36 Hertford Street, Mayfair, the purchase
stops.date_confidence: the Oxford DNB dates the purchase to late 1829; the exact month is not given
stops.campa: With the money from The Disowned and Devereux, and with a good deal more than that money, he buys 36 Hertford Street just off Park Lane and furnishes it extravagantly. He had spent the autumn in lodgings at Vine Cottage in Fulham, hunting for exactly this. It is the address the parliamentary registers will print against his name for years, and the first of a long succession of houses in Mayfair and Park Lane. He stands for St Ives from it, and afterwards for Lincoln.
suggested_refs: History of Parliament Online, 'BULWER, Edward George Lytton Earle (1803-1873), of 36 Hertford Street, Mdx.'
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'

stops.name: Hertford Street, the opening sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; the composition address is inferred from his residence
stops.campa: Paul Clifford appears in three volumes, opening with a highwayman and a long sentence about the weather over London. It is a Newgate novel with an argument in it, that the law manufactures the criminals it then hangs, and it puts the phrase the great unwashed into English on its way past. The argument is disputed while he is alive to defend it, and the novel, read and reprinted and argued over in his lifetime, is forgotten inside a generation of his death. Its first thirty words are not forgotten.
stops.quote: It was a dark and stormy night; the rain fell in torrents, except at occasional intervals, when it was checked by a violent gust of wind which swept up the streets (for it is in London that our scene lies), rattling along the housetops, and fiercely agitating the scanty flame of the lamps that struggled against the darkness.
stops.quote_source: Paul Clifford (1830), opening sentence, verified against the Project Gutenberg text
suggested_refs: The first page of Paul Clifford, three-volume first edition, 1830
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: St Ives, Cornwall, the first seat
stops.date_confidence: contested: Wikipedia's chronology gives St Ives in 1831 and Lincoln from 1832, while a History of Parliament derived summary names Lincoln as the first constituency in 1831. Not resolved here
stops.campa: He enters the House of Commons for the Cornish borough of St Ives, a Reform-minded member in the last unreformed Parliament, elected in the year the Reform Bill is brought in, thrown out, and brought in again. He speaks for the bill. He speaks against the stamp duty on newspapers, which taxes the poor out of the news, and for the right of authors to own what they have written, a subject on which he has figures of his own. Through the same sessions he is producing a novel a year, written in the hours the House leaves him.
suggested_refs: The unreformed borough of St Ives and its electorate on the eve of 1832

stops.name: Lincoln, the reformed seat
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; he holds Lincoln until 1841
stops.campa: The Reform Act redraws the map and returns him for Lincoln, a seat he keeps nine years. He edits the New Monthly Magazine, sits through night divisions, and finishes chapters afterward on whatever hours are left. Eugene Aram appears in this same year: a novel built from a real murder, asking its readers to feel with a scholar who killed a man, and it is attacked from every quarter for asking. He answers the attacks in print, at length. Godolphin and Asmodeus at Large follow the next year.
suggested_refs: Eugene Aram (1832) and the Newgate-novel controversy it deepened
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

segments.name: Italy and the City of the Dead

stops.name: Milan, the Brera and the burning sky
stops.date_confidence: the painting is exhibited at the Brera in 1833 and he sets out for Italy in September of that year; the exact date of the viewing is not recorded
stops.campa: At the Brera hangs an enormous Russian canvas, Karl Bryullov's The Last Day of Pompeii, and Milan has just carried the painter through its streets under a garland. Bulwer-Lytton is travelling south with Rosina on a journey undertaken to repair a marriage, and in Milan he stops in front of it. Figures run under a black sky lit from below. A mother covers a child, a horse rears in falling ash, columns come down out of the dark. The road he is on runs to the place where all of that happened.
suggested_refs: Karl Bryullov, The Last Day of Pompeii, exhibited at the Pinacoteca di Brera, 1833
sources: Getty News, 'Apocalypse Then: Bulwer-Lytton's The Last Days of Pompeii'

stops.name: Naples, the winter with Sir William Gell
stops.date_confidence: the Oxford DNB dates the Italian journey September 1833 to February 1834; some accounts place the writing in the winter of 1832-33 instead
stops.campa: He settles in Naples for the winter and studies with Sir William Gell, the antiquarian whose Pompeiana is the standard account of the excavations. Gell gives him the plans, the street names, the inscriptions painted on the shopfronts, the whole apparatus of a town dug back out of the ground and preserved by the thing that killed it. He takes notes daily. In the same lodgings Rosina, bored, flirts openly with a Neapolitan prince, and they quarrel about it through the winter of the journey they had made to repair the marriage.
suggested_refs: Sir William Gell's Pompeiana, the excavator's handbook the novelist worked from
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'
The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: Pompeii, the excavated forum
stops.date_confidence: the visit falls inside the Italian journey of September 1833 to February 1834; no day recorded
stops.campa: He walks the dug-out streets themselves: the forum, the wheel-ruts worn into the paving, the bakery, the doorway with the mosaic dog. What he writes afterward about that walk is not a description of ruins but a statement of intent. The Last Days of Pompeii will sell as very few English novels of the century sell, and will fix in the general mind a picture of the eruption that archaeology has been correcting ever since. He goes home in February with the manuscript almost finished.
stops.quote: to people once more those deserted streets... to wake to a second existence the City of the Dead
stops.quote_source: Bulwer-Lytton's own preface to The Last Days of Pompeii (1834)
suggested_refs: The forum of Pompeii as excavated in the 1830s
sources: Bulwer-Lytton, preface to The Last Days of Pompeii, quoted in The Victorian Web and in the Project Gutenberg front matter

stops.name: London, Bentley publishes the City of the Dead
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; month not recorded in reachable sources
stops.campa: Richard Bentley publishes The Last Days of Pompeii and it does not stop selling. Glaucus, Ione, the priest Arbaces, and Nydia the blind flower girl who can lead the others out through the ash because darkness has never been an obstacle to her: the last is his own invention and becomes the figure everyone remembers. Two silent films and a Hollywood picture will come out of it. In the same season he brings out The Pilgrims of the Rhine, and the following year Rienzi, the Last of the Roman Tribunes.
suggested_refs: The 1908 Italian silent Gli ultimi giorni di Pompei and the 1935 Schoedsack and Cooper film
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Last Days of Pompeii (1908 film)'

stops.name: The Albany, Piccadilly, the marriage ends in public
stops.date_confidence: the Oxford DNB puts the decision to separate after the Italian journey, so in 1834; the Victorian Web dates the separation 1833 and the legal deed to April 1836
stops.campa: The marriage has been finished since Italy. They come back embittered and recriminatory and agree on a trial separation. In February Rosina comes to his chambers in the Albany and accuses him in public of keeping his mistress Laura Deacon there. In April the separation is made legal by deed: he keeps the children and the income, she keeps a small allowance, and the law of England is on his side in every particular. She will spend forty-four years converting the grievance into print, beginning with a book called A Blighted Life.
stops.quote: Remember, Madame, you have neither father nor brother, and therefore you are completely in my power.
stops.quote_source: Words attributed to him by Rosina Bulwer Lytton in A Blighted Life: A True Story (1880); her account, disputed on his side
suggested_refs: The chambers of the Albany, Piccadilly, in the 1830s
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'
The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'
Project Gutenberg, A Blighted Life: A True Story (ebook 76426)

segments.name: The Stage, the River House, and Knebworth

stops.name: London, Richelieu and the arch-enchanter's wand
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the staging; the exact premiere date is not established in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He has been a baronet for a year, of Knebworth, a house that is still his mother's. He is writing for the stage now, and writing for Macready, who wants large parts. In Richelieu, or the Conspiracy the old cardinal, too frail to lift a sword, draws a circle of church protection around his ward and explains to a soldier what power actually consists of. Macready plays the cardinal in the red robe. The speech comes out of the play whole and is in the language inside a generation.
stops.quote: Beneath the rule of men entirely great, the pen is mightier than the sword. Behold the arch-enchanter's wand! itself a nothing! But taking sorcery from the master-hand to paralyse the Caesars, and to strike the loud earth breathless! Take away the sword; States can be saved without it!
stops.quote_source: Richelieu; Or the Conspiracy (1839), Act II, Scene II, spoken by Cardinal Richelieu
suggested_refs: William Charles Macready in the role of Richelieu
sources: Wikipedia, 'The pen is mightier than the sword'

stops.name: Craven Cottage, Fulham, the riparian retreat
stops.date_confidence: attested; he holds Craven Cottage roughly 1840 to 1846, after taking Vine Cottage in the same neighbourhood in 1829
stops.campa: He takes Craven Cottage on the Thames at Fulham and keeps it six years, an elegant little riparian retreat where the exiled Prince Louis Napoleon is among his guests. He had gone hunting for a London house in this same parish eleven years before, from lodgings at Vine Cottage. He writes at Craven with the river going past below the windows, in rooms got up in a Gothic taste that suits the man about to invent Zanoni. Long after the cottage is gone a football ground covers the site, its old walls somewhere under the centre of the pitch.
suggested_refs: Craven Cottage, Fulham, before the ground was laid over it
sources: Friends of Fulham Palace and Fulham local-history sources
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'

stops.name: Theatre Royal, Haymarket, Money opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Money opens at the Haymarket on the eighth of December, with Macready as Alfred Evelyn, the poor dependent who comes into a fortune and then uses it to find out who had loved him when he had none. It is a comedy about the one subject the English stage of the day will not name straight out, which is why it works, and it is the second leading part he has built for Macready in as many years. He sits in the Commons for Lincoln while it runs. He is thirty-seven, and he has been writing for money since he was twenty-four.
suggested_refs: The Theatre Royal, Haymarket, playbill for 8 December 1840

stops.name: Craven Cottage, Zanoni and the brotherhood
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; the composition address is inferred from his tenancy
stops.campa: Zanoni: an immortal adept of a fraternity that has kept the old wisdom, a young Englishman who wants initiation and is not fit for it, and the Terror closing over Paris in the last volume. He builds the brotherhood out of the Rosicrucian manifestos, out of the legend of Christian Rosenkreuz and the tomb sealed for a hundred and twenty years, and hands the result to the nineteenth century as a three-volume novel. Occultists read it as a coded document. Arthur Edward Waite will spend two books, in 1887 and again in 1924, correcting the Rosicrucian history this novel put into everybody's head.
suggested_refs: Zanoni (1842), first edition, and the Rosicrucian manifestos it drew on
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: Knebworth House, the inheritance and the name
stops.date_confidence: the inheritance attested to 1843; the royal licence for the change of surname attested to 20 February 1844
stops.campa: His mother dies and leaves him Knebworth and the Lytton estate in Hertfordshire, and he writes that he is thoroughly shattered. On the twentieth of February following, by royal licence, he takes the Lytton arms and the compound name he is remembered under, exactly as her will requires. He is forty, and everything she withheld from him while she lived is now his to keep. Over the mantelpiece in her room he has an inscription cut, asking that the room be left as she kept it.
suggested_refs: The inscription over the mantelpiece at Knebworth, asking that Elizabeth Barbara's room be left untouched
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: Great Malvern, the water cure
stops.date_confidence: attested to the decade; the specific year of his Malvern stay is not fixed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He arrives at Great Malvern on the strength of a pamphlet and puts himself for nine or ten weeks into the hands of Dr James Wilson: cold wet sheets before dawn, the douche, long walks on the hills, no wine. The same establishment treats Darwin, Dickens, Carlyle, and Tennyson within a few years of one another, half of literary England soaking in Worcestershire spring water. He takes the cure again at Boppard on the Rhine and at Petersham. What good any of it did him is not recorded, and the diseased ear that will eventually kill him is already troubling him here.
suggested_refs: Wilson and Gully's hydropathic establishment at Great Malvern
sources: Explorethepast.co.uk, Worcestershire Archive and Archaeology Service
The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

segments.name: The Minister, the Colony, and the Asylum

stops.name: Knebworth House, The Caxtons
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: The Caxtons: A Family Picture comes out and it is a different writer altogether: no dandies, no adepts, no doomed cities, only a quiet household, a father with a book he will never finish, and a son who goes to Australia and comes home again. It runs in Blackwood's Magazine first and sells enormously in volume form. The imitator of Byron who came by way of Newgate, Pompeii and the Rosicrucians is writing domestic realism at forty-six, and the age likes him better there.
suggested_refs: The Caxtons (1849), serialised in Blackwood's Magazine

stops.name: Hertford, returned for the county
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; he holds Hertfordshire until his elevation to the peerage in 1866
stops.campa: After eleven years out of Parliament he comes back for the county of Hertfordshire, this time a Conservative. The man who spoke for the Reform Bill from the radical benches now sits opposite them; he has changed his mind about Protection and about a good deal besides, and does not pretend that he has not. He is a county member sitting for the county his mother's family held, four miles from his own park gates, and he holds the seat fourteen years, until a barony takes him out of the Commons.
suggested_refs: The Hertfordshire county election of 1852
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: Glasgow, the Old College on the High Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of election; Wikipedia gives the term as 1856 to 1859, the Victorian Web only the start year
stops.campa: The students of the University of Glasgow elect him Rector, and he goes north to deliver his addresses in the old High Street college, the smoke-blackened seventeenth-century quadrangles the university will abandon for Gilmorehill within twenty years. The rectorship is in the students' gift and is their verdict on the men available to them. Out of the divines and the chemists and the statesmen they choose the novelist. The office is speeches and dinners and nothing else, which is as well, because he can no longer hear a committee. He serves three years.
suggested_refs: The Old College of Glasgow on the High Street, demolished after the move to Gilmorehill
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: Downing Street, the Colonial Office
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the tenure runs 5 June 1858 to 11 June 1859
stops.campa: On the fifth of June he becomes Secretary of State for the Colonies in Lord Derby's government, and takes an office in Downing Street with half the world on the wall. He holds it one year and one week. In that year he makes a Crown colony on the Pacific coast of North America out of a gold rush and a fur company's territory, and names it British Columbia. He sends Colonel Richard Clement Moody and the Royal Engineers out to survey it and lay its towns.
suggested_refs: The old Colonial Office houses on Downing Street, before Scott's building replaced them

stops.name: Hertford, the hustings and the asylum
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the sequence of hustings, committal, and release is dated only by the press coverage of June and July 1858, and no day is fixed
stops.campa: Required by custom to stand again on taking office, he faces the electors of Hertfordshire, and his wife comes to the hustings and denounces him in front of them. Within days he has her seized and committed to a private asylum. He is a cabinet minister, a baronet, and the author of Money; she has neither father nor brother, and the law gives her husband the disposal of her liberty. Then the newspapers take it up, and the public will not have it. She is out again within a few weeks.
stops.quote: I don't believe in any man's friendship; more especially in a mad Doctor's, employed by Sir Edward.
stops.quote_source: Rosina Bulwer Lytton, A Blighted Life: A True Story (1880), verified against the Project Gutenberg text
suggested_refs: The press campaign of summer 1858 that forced Rosina Bulwer Lytton's release
sources: Project Gutenberg, A Blighted Life: A True Story (ebook 76426)

stops.name: Lytton, British Columbia, the name on the map
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the naming; the month is not fixed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Where the Thompson river comes into the Fraser, at the Nlaka'pamux village that the traders' post had overwritten as Fort Dallas, the colony's officers rename the place Lytton, after the minister in London who signed the colony into existence. Miners are working the gravel bars below, and the gold, which is real, is mostly finished inside a decade. He never sails, and never comes within five thousand miles of the canyon that carries his name. The town is still called Lytton.
suggested_refs: Fort Dallas at the confluence of the Thompson and the Fraser, renamed Lytton in 1858

stops.name: Palace of Westminster, Baron Lytton of Knebworth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; day of the patent not recorded in reachable sources
stops.campa: He leaves the Commons after thirty-five years on and off its benches and is created Baron Lytton of Knebworth. The House of Lords acquires a novelist and gets very little use out of him: he is deaf, tired, in pain from the ear that has troubled him for two decades, and increasingly absent. In 1870 they make him a Knight Grand Cross of St Michael and St George. His son Robert, a diplomat who publishes verse as Owen Meredith, will inherit the title and go out to India as Viceroy within a decade.
suggested_refs: The letters patent creating the barony of Lytton of Knebworth, 1866
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: Argyll Hall, Torquay, the house above the sea
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year he takes the house; Argyll Hall, built 1849 on Warren Road, later the Roseland Hotel
stops.campa: He takes a house called Argyll Hall on Warren Road in Torquay, built twenty years before and standing above the rock walk and the bay, and comes there for his health from this year onward. The English Riviera is where invalid England goes: mild air, palm trees, a sea that does not freeze, and doctors who will not be surprised by anything. He is sixty-four and deaf on one side, in more or less constant pain from the ear. At Torquay he goes on working at the pace he set himself at twenty-five.
suggested_refs: Argyll Hall, Warren Road, Torquay, later the Roseland Hotel and now the flats called Marine Palms
sources: English Riviera, 'Writers on the Riviera' itinerary

stops.name: Aldermanbury, the society that claims him
stops.date_confidence: the founding of the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia at Aldermanbury is attested to 1867; his patronage of it is reconstruction, not record
stops.campa: In the City, at Aldermanbury, a small society of Masons founds the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia to study what the Rosicrucian manifestos had actually meant. Its own founding record does not name him. Within a few years the occult revival is calling him the order's patron, its Grand Patron, its secret adept, on the strength of Zanoni and of nothing anybody can produce. What he is, in the year they begin saying it, is a deaf peer of the realm at Torquay who once wrote a novel about initiates.
suggested_refs: The founding minutes of the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia, which do not name him

stops.name: Knebworth House, the study, The Coming Race
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1871, published anonymously by Blackwood; retitled Vril: The Power of the Coming Race only from 1873
stops.campa: In the study at Knebworth he writes a short novel about an engineer who falls down a mine shaft into a lit world under the ground, where a tall, calm, winged people have mastered one force that does everything: it heals, it kills, it lights, it moves, it persuades. He calls the force vril, and tells a friend he means by it electricity dimly guessed at. Blackwood publishes the book anonymously in May, without his name anywhere on it, and it runs through eight editions in eighteen months.
stops.quote: There is no word in any language I know which is an exact synonym for vril. I should call it electricity, except that it comprehends in its manifold branches other forces of nature, to which, in our scientific nomenclature, differing names are assigned, such as magnetism, galvanism, &c.
stops.quote_source: The Coming Race (1871), Chapter VII, verified against the Project Gutenberg text
suggested_refs: The study at Knebworth House; the anonymous Blackwood first edition of The Coming Race
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'

stops.name: Torquay, the death at Argyll Hall
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; cause given as a cerebral abscess following chronic middle-ear disease
stops.campa: He dies at Argyll Hall on the eighteenth of January, four months short of seventy, of an abscess in the brain arising from the diseased ear that had deafened and tormented him for twenty years. Robert had come down to Torquay with his wife the year before to see him. Kenelm Chillingly is at the printers: its first impression, three thousand one hundred and fifty sets in three volumes, sells out on the day of publication, days after the author's death. The Parisians follows the same year, and the unfinished Pausanias the Spartan in 1876.
suggested_refs: Kenelm Chillingly, published days after his death and sold out on the day
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'
The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the Chapel of St Edmund
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Dean Stanley hesitates over the burial. John Forster presses him, arguing that if a writer of this standing is refused, nobody can ever be admitted; a letter in The Times follows, and the Dean consents. He is not laid in Poets' Corner. Stanley puts him in the Chapel of St Edmund, beside the tomb of Sir Humphrey Bourchier, killed at Barnet four hundred years before, who walks through one of his own romances as a character. He had asked to be buried simply at Knebworth.
stops.quote_source: Gravestone inscription, Chapel of St Edmund, Westminster Abbey
suggested_refs: The gravestone in St Edmund's Chapel, recording the parliamentary career and the 'genius as an author'
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Chronology'

segments.name: After: the Word Gets Out of the Book

stops.name: Whitehall, the figure in niche S05
stops.date_confidence: the placement date of 1874 comes from vanderkrogt.net and londonremembers and could not be independently re-verified; the building itself dates 1861-1868
stops.campa: On the front of George Gilbert Scott's new Colonial Office in Whitehall, the secretaries of state go up into their niches, Henry Hugh Armstead's stone figures looking down into the street. Bulwer-Lytton takes niche S05, a year after his death, commemorating an office he had actually held in the shabby old houses the building replaced. Those who look closely at the face report that it resembles his son Robert, Viceroy of India, more than it resembles him.
suggested_refs: Henry Hugh Armstead's series of colonial secretaries on the Whitehall facade, niche S05
sources: vanderkrogt.net, 'Sculptures at the Foreign and Commonwealth Office'

stops.name: London, bos and vril
stops.date_confidence: contested: the renaming is widely dated 1886 with the trademark in 1887, while other accounts give 1884; the company Bovril Ltd is formed in 1889
stops.campa: John Lawson Johnston, a Scot who has been supplying the French army with beef extract, needs a better name than Johnston's Fluid Beef for the thick brown paste in the jar. He takes bos, the Latin ox, and welds it to vril, the world-force of a novel published fifteen years earlier by a peer now three years dead. The name is trademarked in 1887 and the company formed in 1889. It goes into every kitchen in Britain, and people drink it hot when they have a cold.
suggested_refs: Early Bovril jars and advertising, carrying half of Bulwer-Lytton's coinage into the grocery trade
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Lytton, Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer'

stops.name: 17 Lansdowne Road, Holland Park, vril becomes a fact
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of completion of The Secret Doctrine
stops.campa: In a house in Holland Park, Helena Blavatsky finishes The Secret Doctrine on the twentieth of October. Vril passes into it, not as a novelist's coinage but as a real force known to the ancients and since forgotten, and as evidence that the fiction had been dictated by a knowledge its author only half possessed. The Theosophists correct him after his death, making him an initiate who said more than he knew he was saying. He had said, while he was alive to be asked, that he meant electricity.
stops.quote: this fluid is capable of being raised and disciplined into the mightiest agency over all forms of matter, animate or inanimate. It can destroy like the flash of lightning; yet, differently applied, it can replenish or invigorate life, heal, and preserve.
stops.quote_source: The Coming Race (1871), verified against the Project Gutenberg text
suggested_refs: The Secret Doctrine (1888), in which vril is treated as recovered fact

stops.name: Munich, the circle takes the word
stops.date_confidence: as carried in maria_orsic.journey.json; the historical existence of a Vril Gesellschaft is treated by historians as pseudohistory, its earliest identifiable source Willy Ley's sceptical article of 1947
stops.campa: In Munich, Maria Orsic and a companion called Traute name their circle the Vril Gesellschaft and take the word directly out of the novel, forty-eight years after an English lord invented it in a Hertfordshire study. What they mean by it is a power lying under the earth, a race of masters, and a Germany that could be handed both. Nothing in The Coming Race supports that reading. Its underground people intend to come up and supplant the races on the surface, and the man telling the story is frightened of them throughout. The circle keeps the word.
stops.quote: The fire lodged in the hollow of a rod directed by the hand of a child could shatter the strongest fortress, or cleave its burning way from the van to the rear of an embattled host.
stops.quote_source: The Coming Race (1871), Chapter IX, verified against the Project Gutenberg text
suggested_refs: Willy Ley, 'Pseudoscience in Naziland' (1947), the earliest identifiable source for the Vril Society claim

stops.name: San Jose, the worst opening sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of founding; the contest ran annually until Scott Rice discontinued it in January 2025
stops.campa: Professor Scott Rice of San Jose State University invites the public to compose the worst possible opening sentence to an imaginary novel, and names the competition after the man who wrote It was a dark and stormy night. Entrants are asked for one sentence only, and it has to be bad on purpose. Thousands send one in every year for four decades. The best-selling English novelist of his generation, Secretary of State for the Colonies, Baron Lytton of Knebworth, is now most often met with as the name of that contest. Rice closes it in January 2025, citing his age.
suggested_refs: The Bulwer-Lytton Fiction Contest, 1982 to 2024
